title: Glendale, Colorado well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Glendale area wells show a 28 ft median depth and 15 gpm median yield. Here’s what that means for drilling and buying property near Denver.
h1: Understanding water wells around Glendale, Colorado
intro_html:
Glendale sits in the Denver urban area, so most of the 9,590 nearby well permits are for monitoring and municipal work, not rural homes. The numbers still tell you how deep water tends to be, how much it produces, and what a private well is likely to cost in this part of the Denver Basin.

If you’re buying or planning to build in places like Holly Hills, Four Square Mile, or over toward Cherry Hills Village or Englewood, it helps to read these stats like a driller would, not like a brochure.

sections.heading: How deep wells run around Glendale
sections.html:
Within about 5 miles of Glendale, the median total depth is only 28 feet, with the middle half of wells between 20 and 45 feet. About 91% of wells are under 100 feet, and only 3% are between 100 and 300 feet. A small share reach 300–600 feet (2%), and 4% go beyond 600 feet, with the deepest at 2,102 feet.

That very shallow median reflects a heavy mix of monitoring wells in alluvial and Denver Basin sediments. A private household well here could be either a shallow alluvial setup or a deeper Denver aquifer well, depending on location and water-rights issues, so don’t assume your well will match the 28-foot median.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water these wells make
sections.html:
Of the wells that report production, the median yield is 15.0 gpm, with the middle half between 8.2 and 113.0 gpm. About 55% of tested wells report 15 gpm or more, 28% fall in the 5–15 gpm band, 13% come in at 1–5 gpm, and only 4% are under 1 gpm.

For a typical exempt household well in this region, 15 gpm is more than enough for normal use and some irrigation. The 4% under 1 gpm are the ones that behave like problem wells; you want to know if any nearby domestic wells fall in that low-yield group before you close on a lot.

sections.heading: Water table depth and trend near Glendale
sections.html:
Static water levels are generally shallow here. The median depth to water is 15 feet, with the middle half between 11 and 22 feet below the surface. That’s consistent with alluvial and shallow Denver Basin conditions along the Denver metro corridor.

Looking by decade, the median measured water level was 14 feet in the 2010s and 15 feet in the 2020s. That one-foot change over recent decades does not suggest a big regional drop in groundwater levels in the dataset, though individual wells can still see local declines or seasonal swings.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and permit history
sections.html:
Well permitting around Glendale ramped up sharply in the 1990s and 2000s. The records show 143 permits in the 1950s, 120 in the 1960s, and 151 in the 1970s, then a jump to 361 in the 1980s. Activity really takes off with 2,604 permits in the 1990s and 2,461 in the 2000s, then 1,415 in the 2010s and 583 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit is from 2025.

Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 4,387 wells, Ground Exploration LLC (Bender, Joseph T.) on 333, and Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.) on 125. About 7,714 wells list unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, 499 list Alluvial, and 208 name the Denver aquifer, with 100% counted as Denver Basin aquifer wells in the records.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
Glendale sits over Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, where typical drilling runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the local 28-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone pencils out to roughly $1,400–$2,000. By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished well in that depth range usually ends up around $7,400–$14,000.

If your specific site needs a deeper Denver aquifer completion instead of a shallow alluvial well, your footage and cost climb quickly. That’s why it’s important to have a driller price your well on expected depth for your exact parcel, not just a neighborhood average.

sections.heading: Environmental and low-yield risks to watch
sections.html:
This area is data-rich for monitoring. About 70% of permits within 5 miles are for monitoring use, and there are 700 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 186 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles. That doesn’t mean every private well is contaminated, but it does mean you should take water quality seriously.

Ask for recent lab testing on any existing well and plan to retest regularly. On a new well, build a good surface seal and keep septic systems and de-icing or industrial areas away from the wellhead. Also check for any nearby wells in the 4% under 1 gpm category, since that hints at localized low-yield conditions.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot near Glendale
sections.html:
Before you buy a lot in Glendale, Holly Hills, Four Square Mile, or the nearby unincorporated pockets, pull the well permits around it. You want to see typical depths, yields, and which aquifer is being used. With the local median depth at 28 feet and median yield at 15.0 gpm, many sites look promising, but urban water-rights and augmentation rules can still complicate new wells.

Confirm that a new exempt household-use well is actually allowed and that its location works with your building envelope and septic layout. For an existing home, get the well log, pump test data if available, and a full water quality panel, especially given the density of monitoring and cleanup sites in the Denver area.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around Glendale, Colorado?
faq.a: Within about 5 miles of Glendale, the median well depth is 28 feet, and the middle half of wells run between 20 and 45 feet deep. About 91% of wells are under 100 feet, while only a small share extend beyond 300 feet and a few reach more than 600 feet, including one at 2,102 feet. Domestic wells may differ depending on site and aquifer choice.

faq.q: How much water do Glendale, CO wells typically produce?
faq.a: Reported pump tests near Glendale show a median yield of 15.0 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 8.2 and 113.0 gpm. Around 55% of wells report 15 gpm or more, 28% fall between 5 and 15 gpm, 13% are in the 1–5 gpm range, and about 4% come in under 1 gpm. That’s generally adequate for normal household use.

faq.q: What is the water table depth near Glendale, Colorado?
faq.a: Static water level data show a median depth to water of 15 feet, with the middle half between 11 and 22 feet below ground. By decade, the median was 14 feet in the 2010s and 15 feet in the 2020s, which doesn’t indicate a strong long-term decline in the dataset, though individual wells can respond differently to pumping and seasonal changes.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well near Glendale, CO?
faq.a: In the Glendale area, drilling in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock typically runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the local 28-foot median depth, the borehole alone is around $1,400–$2,000, and a complete well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical generally totals about $7,400–$14,000. Deeper Denver aquifer wells will cost more due to extra footage and materials.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Glendale and nearby Denver areas?
faq.a: Water quality varies by site. Around Glendale there are 700 PFAS sampling or contamination locations and 186 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, and about 70% of local wells are monitoring wells. Many private wells still produce good water, but you should always review any existing lab results and run your own comprehensive water test before relying on a well.
